books.section: Topic 2.5 Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans

options.misconception: The passage says the opposite — converts remained second-class citizens.
options.text: The English welcomed any Native person who converted to Christianity as a full equal
Conversion alone did not bring acceptance, because the English demanded complete abandonment of Native traditions

options.misconception: The passage says nothing about literacy; Eliot's converts did learn to read.
options.text: The English believed Native peoples could never learn to read or write

rationales.A: The passage says the opposite — converts remained second-class citizens.
rationales.B: The passage gives the test the English applied: converts were “judged by how completely they had abandoned their old ways.” That is a test no convert could pass at once — and many could never pass at all, because the English kept moving the line. The second-class status of praying Indians shows that conversion was not enough for the English: what they wanted was not new Christians but new Englishmen, and Native birth itself remained a mark against them.
rationales.C: The passage says nothing about literacy; Eliot's converts did learn to read.
rationales.D: The towns were real — fourteen of them existed by the 1670s.
rationales.general:
1. Find the test the English applied. Converts were judged by how completely they had abandoned their old ways.
2. Ask whether conversion passed the test. It did not — converts remained second-class citizens.
3. Name what the English really wanted. Not new Christians, but new Englishmen — and Native birth stayed a mark against them.
Remember: when a group is judged by what it has given up, belonging is a moving target, not a door.

source: original; stimulus is an original secondary passage written for this question
stem: The passage states that even converted Native peoples in the praying towns remained second-class citizens. Which of the following best explains what that fact shows about English attitudes?

stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, summarizing standard background on the praying towns and French missions.
stimulus.text: In Massachusetts Bay, Puritan ministers built “praying towns” — villages where Native converts lived under English law, dressed in European clothing, and were expected to give up their own customs. By the 1670s there were fourteen such towns. Yet even converted Native peoples remained second-class citizens in English eyes: they were judged by how completely they had abandoned their old ways. French Jesuit missionaries took the opposite approach, living among Native peoples and accepting that Christianity could blend with Native traditions.
